body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Jang (food)
Great culinary craft is applied chemistry in motion, and Jang (food) proves it. From raw ingredients to temperature control, tiny structural changes transform flavor and texture.

Jang is a category of sauce in Korean cuisine, generally fermented and made of soybeans. The three main types are ganjang, (soy sauce), doenjang (soy paste), and gochujang (chili paste). Jang is a central element of Korean cuisine, widely used as an ingredient, seasoning, or dipping sauce.

Ganjang, doenjang, and gochujang are often produced in an annual batch. It involves multiple stages of fermentation over months, using jars known as jangdok. The main ingredient is meju, a dried block of soybeans. Meju is placed in a brine solution, forming a solid, which becomes doenjang, and a liquid, which becomes ganjang. Gochujang is made by combining powdered meju, Korean chili pepper, and other ingredients. Other varieties include cheonggukjang, simply consisting of fermented soybeans, as well as various combinations of jangs, including ssamjang.

The fermentation of jang, driven by various bacteria and fungi, develops amino acids and peptides that result in a complex flavor. Industrial products have simpler flavors as their fermentation is more controlled. Jang is salty and is used to flavor most Korean side dishes. It is a typical component of a Korean meal.
